A blog excerpt notes that Trafaria is a parish capital on which Costa de Caparica also depends, with a view of the Tagus river.

The club promoted sailing as a sport and built affordable boat models in its own premises, offering easy terms to buy them.

items.action: Dune and sea dynamics created emerged sands where bathers' huts appeared at the far west of Almada municipality.
Growing numbers of Lisbon bathers reached south-bank beaches; Trafaria beach was easily reached by boat but could not grow further.
items.conditions: consolidated urban nucleus without room to grow

items.action: A river ferry link departing from Belém served a popular bathing zone with cheap lodging, called the 'praia dos tesos'.
items.conditions: Costa da Caparica over four km from Trafaria with less affordable lodging

items.action: In early decades, seasonal occupation adapted to dune advance and retreat by relocating existing structures; this reversed as buildings consolidated from the 1970s.
items.conditions: advance and retreat of the dune ridge

items.action: According to tradition, fishermen from Ílhavo in the north first settled the previously deserted Costa da Caparica, followed immediately by fishermen from the Algarve, bringing their fishing organisation and customs.
Early fishermen stayed only for the fishing season, living in small huts that they set on fire when leaving for home.
items.conditions: fishing season (safra) in October, November and December

items.action: Settlement became permanent: Ílhavo people lived to the north on a rise near the present fishermen's huts, Algarvians to the south, each in separate quarters.
Algarvians sheltered in huts of esparto grass or rush, like those at home; Ílhavo fishermen's traditional dwelling is a plank-walled palheiro with only the roof thatched.

Eighteenth- and nineteenth-century accounts mention only straw huts at Caparica; the author suggests Ílhavo settlers copied Algarvian huts because timber was scarce and costly, though plank houses may have existed early.
items.conditions: timber hard and expensive to obtain

items.action: Ílhavo people were first to live permanently at Caparica; Algarvians returned to the Algarve when the season ended.
Two Ílhavo and two Algarvian fishing masters settled with their crews in more comfortable huts; other masters followed in later years, partly to keep their fishing grounds.
items.conditions: in 1770 the beach had few year-round residents; Algarvians feared losing their fishing zone

numbers.what: year-round settled masters in first group

items.who: mestres da pesca Joaquim Pedro, José Rapaz, José Gonçalves Bexiga, Romualdo dos

items.action: Rivalry between Ílhavo and Algarvian fishermen was strong, with the northerners dominant; the old quarter's houses resemble those of Costa Nova more than the Algarve, and the groups eventually merged.
items.conditions: rivalry survives in children's North versus South games

items.action: Costa da Caparica counted 307 heads of family, mostly descended from northerners.
Northern pioneers built a church of rush and planks early on; the local cemetery dates from 1780 and was walled in 1848.
The first stone-and-lime house was built; King João VI stayed there when visiting Caparica, and the owner added the royal arms, giving it the name casa da Coroa.
items.conditions: it was the only such house in the place then

items.action: Great fires destroyed many huts at Costa da Caparica, including the fire called 'Quinquilheira' in 1840.
Around 1900 Costa da Caparica was still a camp of huts; one source says the only mixed stone-and-wood house was a tavern, which the editor disputes, citing masonry buildings by 1859.
Caparica fishing settlement mixed plank-built houses with straw-roofed huts; some huts were built on disused boats, shown in Roque Gameiro watercolours, with horizontal planking and straw roofs.
Plank-built housing grew while old Algarve-style straw huts died out, as places frequented by summer visitors developed quickly.
Agro Ferreira described the settlement before 1922 as about a hundred thatch huts, some dozens of brick huts and half a dozen stone-and-lime huts.
Raul Brandão's account implied the fishermen's houses were plank-built with dark thatch roofs.
Leite de Vasconcelos noted many wooden thatched houses were being replaced by good dwellings; he described roofs of pine or chestnut beams, canes and bundles of esparto tied with twine.
An old photograph shows a few plank huts among many Algarve-style esparto huts scattered on the sand.
Today no straw huts survive; the old fishermen's quarter has single-storey plank houses with gable doors facing the street and Marseille tile roofs.
Settlers from Ílhavo did not use the pile-dwelling construction typical of their homeland and their other settlements at Caparica.
Fonte da Telha was a fishing hamlet made of primitive huts used for storage, animal shelter and housing.

numbers.what: distance south of Costa da Caparica

items.action: Caparica fishermen sometimes hauled drag nets ashore at Fonte da Telha and slept in dune pits sheltered with bent esparto like small tents.
items.gear: drag nets (redes de arrasto); esparto cover

items.action: Fonte da Telha emerged as a settlement when the fishermen decided to stay permanently and built huts copying those of Caparica.
Fonte da Telha huts keep a primitive character; wall structure uses posts called muletas driven into the sand, low side posts rising little over 1.50 m.

numbers.what: height of side-wall posts above ground

items.action: Builders lay roof beams from wall plate to ridge and fasten single or paired canes across them; wall battens are similar but more widely spaced.
Esparto-style cladding (estorno) is stitched on; a transverse row at the ridge is secured by canes, topped by a combreira; interior walls get horizontal boarding.
Fonte da Telha, growing as a bathing beach, is changing: estorno huts are quickly replaced by board or hard-material houses in regular streets, though a few huts remain.
Primitive Costa da Caparica huts, a large part of the settlement until the early 1900s, are now known only through Fonte da Telha examples.
Huts similar to those elsewhere on the coast existed at Trafaria before 1793, of long wild straw or palm leaves with outer mud walls.
Saveiros leaving the coast south of Trafaria used a noted sheltered cove between the Tagus banks and rocks, where they lived quartered most of the year in cabins.
Fishermen of master Reguinga's crew, after their boat capsized, were rescued by master Vitorino José da Silva's crew once they invoked Our Lady of the Rosary.
items.conditions: after a capsizing (virada), second half of September
items.who: pescadores da companha do mestre Reguinga; companha do mestre Vitorino José da S

items.action: The two masters held a large festival with money raised at Ribeira Nova and the beach fish auctions; their successors continued it.
items.who: mestres Reguinga and Vitorino José da Silva and their successors

items.action: In an alternative account, master Manuel Reguinga's shipwreck occurred on 1 July 1824, and the festivals were afterwards held in September.
The festival of Our Lady of the Rosary was held in September until 1929, then resumed for some years after 1937.
The festivals for Our Lady of the Rosary were already being celebrated in 1888, according to an archive record.
The Ponta do Cabedelo is described as a place only for contemplation and maintenance of an existing radio beacon, reached by a path off the road.
The author suggests the cabedelo formed a sea inlet around 1750, disputing the myth that the 1755 earthquake deposited the Costa's sand.
